questions.question: Applications are often classed as data-intensive or compute-intensive. For a data-intensive application, which resource is rarely the limiting factor, and what usually is?

options.text: Network bandwidth is rarely limiting; the number of CPU threads available to the process usually is
Raw CPU power is rarely limiting; the data's volume, complexity, and rate of change usually are
Disk capacity is rarely limiting; the speed of floating-point computation usually is
Data volume is rarely limiting; raw CPU power for computation usually is

questions.explanation: A data-intensive application is one whose hard problems come from its data: how much there is, how complex it is, and how fast it changes. Raw CPU power is rarely what limits it. A compute-intensive workload, such as a numerical simulation, is the opposite case where processor speed dominates. Reversing the two, or naming some other single hardware resource, misses that the bottleneck is managing the data itself.

questions.question: In a data-intensive application, which of these are typically bigger problems than raw CPU power? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The amount of data
The complexity of data
The cost of CPU cycles
The speed at which the data is changing

questions.explanation: Data-intensive applications are limited by their data rather than by computation: the amount of data, the complexity of data, and the speed at which it changes. Each is a separate axis of growth, so a system can be strained by one without the others. CPU cost is the classic compute-intensive concern, and raw CPU power is rarely the limiting factor for data-intensive work.

optionExplanations.a: Data volume is a primary data-intensive challenge because storage, transfer, indexing, and processing work all grow as the dataset grows. Treating capacity as merely a CPU problem misses those separate resource pressures.
optionExplanations.b: Complex data creates difficult relationships, representations, and access patterns even when its byte count is modest. More processor cycles alone do not remove the modeling and coordination complexity.
optionExplanations.c: Raw CPU power is rarely the limiting factor for data-intensive applications, which is what separates them from compute-intensive ones. CPU cost can matter in a particular system, but it is not one of the typical data-driven bottlenecks.
optionExplanations.d: A high rate of change stresses ingestion, indexing, replication, and the freshness of derived results. It is a distinct growth axis from both the amount of stored data and the complexity of its structure.

questions.question: Which building block serves the need to remember the result of an expensive operation, to speed up reads?

options.text: Search indexes
Batch processing
Caches
Stream processing

questions.explanation: A cache remembers the result of an expensive operation, such as a slow query or computation, so later reads can be served from the stored result instead of recomputing it. A search index serves keyword search and filtering, stream processing hands messages to another process asynchronously, and batch processing periodically crunches a large amount of accumulated data. Only the cache exists specifically to speed up repeated reads of an already-computed result.

questions.question: As a building block of a data-intensive application, what need does a database serve?

options.text: Data remains available only while its original process is running
Data written now can be found later by the same or another application
Data can be recovered only by an operator restoring a backup
Every read sees the latest write, even when many clients update the data at once

questions.explanation: A database stores data so that the same application, or another application, can find it again later. That separates writing from later reading: the reader need not be the process that originally stored the data, and the data outlives that process. Guarantees about what concurrent readers see (consistency) and about restoring data from backups are separate concerns, not the basic purpose of the building block.

questions.question: Databases, caches, search indexes, stream processing, and batch processing are standard building blocks of data-intensive applications. Why does listing them sound obvious to most engineers?

options.text: Because the list is deliberately simplified for readers who are new to data systems
Because most engineers have written a storage engine themselves at some point
Because the abstraction is so successful we use these tools without thinking
Because vendors market these categories so heavily that every engineer knows them

questions.explanation: These data systems are such a successful abstraction that engineers use them all the time without thinking much about them. Most engineers would never write a new storage engine from scratch, because existing databases do the job well. The obviousness is a sign of the abstraction's success, not of simplification for beginners or of vendor marketing.

questions.question: Standard building blocks such as databases, caches, and queues are a successful abstraction. Which two difficulties still remain when you build an application from them? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Choice — many systems with differing characteristics, because applications differ in requirements
Combination — tools must be stitched together when one cannot do the whole job alone
Cost — licensing fees for data tools dominate the budget of most projects
Staffing — too few engineers understand how storage engines actually work inside

questions.explanation: Two difficulties remain. Choice: there are many databases, caching approaches, and search-index designs with different characteristics, because applications have different requirements, so you must decide which fits. Combination: when one tool cannot do the whole job, several must be stitched together with application code, which in effect makes the application developer a designer of a new composite data system.

optionExplanations.a: Different applications need different guarantees and access patterns, so databases, caches, and queues with different characteristics are not interchangeable. The abstraction is successful, but choosing the right implementation still requires judgment.
optionExplanations.b: A single tool often cannot provide every required storage, search, caching, and messaging behavior. Application code must then compose several components and take responsibility for the guarantees of the combined system.
optionExplanations.c: Licensing can affect a project budget, but it is not an architectural difficulty that follows from using standard building blocks. The real problems are selecting and combining tools, and those apply equally to open-source tools with no license fee.
optionExplanations.d: Knowledge of engine internals can help, but a shortage of such specialists is not what makes building from standard blocks hard. Successful abstractions exist precisely so that most application engineers need not implement storage engines themselves.

questions.question: A database and a message queue both store data for some time, yet they are very different categories. Which two reasons justify lumping them together as 'data systems' anyway? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The boundaries between the categories have blurred
Both guarantee durability for every message they accept
Applications increasingly need several tools stitched together
Both expose the same delivery semantics to their clients

questions.explanation: Boundaries between categories have blurred, and applications increasingly need several tools stitched together to meet their requirements. Neither durability nor delivery semantics is the reason — those differ sharply between a database and a queue.

optionExplanations.a: Modern products blur old categories: Redis can serve as both a datastore and a queue, while Kafka combines messaging with database-like durability. That overlap makes the broader term “data system” useful.
optionExplanations.b: Durability guarantees vary substantially by product and configuration; a queue may lose messages and a database may offer different durability levels. A universal durability guarantee therefore cannot justify grouping the categories.
optionExplanations.c: Demanding applications commonly combine databases, caches, indexes, and queues behind one service interface. Grouping them as data systems highlights that the application must coordinate the whole composite.
optionExplanations.d: Databases and message queues deliberately expose different access and delivery semantics—for example, querying stored state versus consuming messages. Their sameness is not the reason for the shared category.

questions.question: You add a Memcached caching layer and an Elasticsearch server alongside your main database. Whose responsibility is it to keep them in sync?

options.text: The database's replication subsystem
The application code's
The cache's write-through policy
The operations team's monitoring

questions.explanation: The application owns the synchronization logic because Memcached, Elasticsearch, and the primary database do not automatically share one consistency model. Once several general-purpose tools are composed behind one API, the application must define how updates propagate and what guarantees users receive.

questions.question: An application combines a database, a cache, and a search index behind its own service API. What is the main consequence for the developer?

options.text: The weakest component's guarantees automatically propagate to the whole composite service
You can stop reasoning about the guarantees of the individual tools altogether
Overall performance becomes simply the sum of the components' performance
Your composite service makes guarantees of its own, making you a data system designer

questions.explanation: The API hides the individual tools from clients, so the combination is in effect a new, special-purpose data system built from general-purpose components. Clients rely on the guarantees of that composite, for example that the cache is correctly invalidated or updated on writes so they see consistent results. The developer must therefore design and uphold those guarantees, becoming a data system designer as well as an application developer. Guarantees do not combine automatically, and performance is not simply additive.

questions.question: Over time, many different people in engineering and operations will work on a system, both keeping its current behaviour running and adapting it to new use cases. Which system concern is about letting all of them work on it productively?

options.text: Reliability
Scalability
Maintainability
Operability

questions.explanation: Maintainability is defined in terms of the people who work on the system over its lifetime, both maintaining current behaviour and adapting it to new use cases. Reliability is about working correctly despite faults, and scalability about coping with growth in load. Operability is narrower: it is one of maintainability's three design principles (with simplicity and evolvability) and focuses on the operations team keeping the system running.

questions.question: In software systems, what does reliability mean, in short?

options.text: Never failing under any circumstances
Working correctly despite faults
Recovering quickly after a failure
Meeting the targets written into a service level agreement

questions.explanation: Reliability roughly means continuing to work correctly, even when things go wrong. It does not mean that faults never happen, since no system can eliminate every fault; it means faults are tolerated so the system keeps working. Fast recovery after a failure and meeting an SLA are related goals, but neither is the definition: a system can meet an SLA by luck, and recovering after a failure means the failure already happened.

questions.question: Which expectation belongs to what it means for software to be 'working correctly', even though it is often overlooked when people think about reliability?

options.text: Using no more hardware than a competitor
Having a user interface that requires no training
Being implemented in a memory-safe language
Preventing unauthorized access and abuse

questions.explanation: Security is part of correctness: a system is not working correctly if unauthorized people can read, alter, or abuse its data. Correctness also includes performing the expected function, tolerating misuse, and meeting required performance under expected load.

questions.question: In reliability terms, how do a fault and a failure differ?

options.text: A fault is a user mistake; a failure is a hardware or network problem
A fault is transient and recoverable; a failure is permanent and needs manual repair
A fault is a component deviating from spec; a failure is the system ceasing service
A fault is caught by internal monitoring; a failure is one that customers report to you

questions.explanation: A fault is one component of the system deviating from its spec; a failure is the system as a whole stopping providing the required service to the user. Because the probability of a fault can never be reduced to zero, the design goal is fault-tolerance mechanisms that stop faults from turning into failures. The distinction is about scope (one component versus the whole service), not about who caused it, whether it is transient, or how it was detected.

questions.question: Why is the term 'fault-tolerant' slightly misleading?

options.text: Because tolerating a fault implies the fault was anticipated in the design
Because no system tolerates every kind of fault, so the claim must be scoped
Because it describes an aspiration that no real system has ever achieved
Because it comes from hardware engineering and misleads applied to software

questions.explanation: The term suggests a system could tolerate every possible kind of fault, which is not feasible. For example, tolerating the whole planet being destroyed would require hosting servers in space. So it only makes sense to say a system tolerates certain named types of faults, such as a disk failure or the loss of one machine. The term is still used; the claim simply has to be scoped.

questions.question: Why can it make sense to deliberately increase the rate of faults in a fault-tolerant system?

options.text: To keep rarely run error-handling code exercised, as Chaos Monkey does
To lower the mean time to failure of the individual components
To produce the fault records that compliance audits require
To make high-percentile response time measurements more representative

questions.explanation: Many critical bugs are due to poor error handling, and error-handling code runs rarely, so its bugs can go unnoticed. Deliberately triggering faults, for example by randomly killing individual processes without warning as Netflix's Chaos Monkey does, keeps the fault-tolerance machinery continually exercised and tested. That raises confidence that real faults will be handled correctly when they occur naturally.

questions.question: Which kind of fault is usually better prevented than merely tolerated, and why?

options.text: Hardware faults, because they occur independently on each machine
Human error, because people remain the least predictable component
Software bugs, because the same bug is present on every node at once
Security, because a breach of sensitive data cannot be undone

questions.explanation: Security breaches are exceptional because disclosure of sensitive data is irreversible: recovery cannot make an attacker forget data already obtained. Fault tolerance is most useful when damage can be contained or repaired; for irreversible compromise, prevention is the priority.

questions.question: Hard disks are reported to have an MTTF of about 10 to 50 years. On a storage cluster with 10,000 disks, what should you expect?

options.text: One disk to die per week
One disk to die per day
One disk to die per hour
One disk to die per month

questions.explanation: 10,000 disks at a 10-year MTTF implies about 2.7 failures per day; at 50 years it implies about 0.55 per day. Thus, a fleet of this size should expect roughly one disk failure per day even though each disk individually lasts for years.

questions.question: Which of these are hardware-redundancy measures? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Disks in a RAID configuration
Dual power supplies and hot-swappable CPUs
Batteries and diesel generators for backup power
Checksums in application code to detect corrupted records

questions.explanation: Hardware redundancy means duplicating physical components so a spare can take over while a broken one is replaced: RAID for disks, dual power supplies and hot-swappable CPUs for servers, and batteries and diesel generators for datacenter power. Checksums are a software technique that only detects corruption. Hardware redundancy cannot completely prevent hardware problems from causing failures, but it is well understood and can often keep a single machine running for years.

optionExplanations.a: RAID adds redundant disks or redundant data placement so a single disk failure need not stop access. It is a hardware-level availability measure, although multiple failures or controller faults can still defeat it.
optionExplanations.b: A second power supply lets the server keep running if one supply fails, and hot-swappable CPUs can be replaced while the machine stays up. Both work by duplicating or replacing physical parts, rather than by software detecting a fault.
optionExplanations.c: Batteries and diesel generators provide alternate physical power sources when grid power fails. They reduce a datacenter-level hardware dependency but cannot prevent every possible outage.
optionExplanations.d: A checksum is computed and checked by software to detect corrupted bytes; it does not provide another disk, CPU, or power source. Detection may enable recovery from a replica, but the checksum itself is not hardware redundancy.

questions.question: For a long time, redundant hardware components within each machine were enough for most applications, and multi-machine redundancy was needed only where high availability was essential. Which condition made that acceptable?

options.text: That the application served fewer than a hundred concurrent users
That you can restore a backup onto a new machine fairly quickly
That the disks were enterprise-grade rather than consumer models
That the datacenter had two fully independent power feeds

questions.explanation: Component redundancy made total failure of a single machine fairly rare. When it did happen, you could restore a backup onto a new machine fairly quickly, so the downtime was not catastrophic for most applications. Only applications for which high availability was absolutely essential needed redundancy across machines. The argument rested on fast restore, not on user counts, disk grade, or power feeds.

questions.question: Which two trends broke the 'hardware redundancy is enough' assumption? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Data volumes and appetite for computing grew, so more machines means more faults
Cloud platforms favour elasticity over single-machine reliability, so instances vanish
Disks became fundamentally less reliable than they were in the 1990s
Virtualization made single-machine failure rates impossible to measure

questions.explanation: Two trends weakened the single-machine-redundancy argument. Larger systems use more machines, so component faults become routine at fleet scale; cloud instances may also disappear without warning. Software fault tolerance additionally permits rolling maintenance by moving work while nodes are patched or replaced.

optionExplanations.a: As fleets grow, even low per-machine failure rates produce frequent failures somewhere in the system. Redundancy confined to one machine is therefore insufficient; software must tolerate losing whole machines.
optionExplanations.b: Elastic clouds treat instances as replaceable and may withdraw them with little warning. That design favors moving work among machines rather than relying on each individual machine to remain continuously available.
optionExplanations.c: The argument does not depend on disks suddenly becoming intrinsically worse than 1990s disks. The important change is fleet scale: many components turn rare individual faults into routine aggregate events.
optionExplanations.d: Virtualization does not make failure rates unknowable, and it is not why hardware redundancy became insufficient. The relevant cloud property is that instances are replaceable and sometimes disappear, which creates the need for software fault tolerance.

questions.question: Why might adding identical replicas fail to protect a service from a software fault?

options.text: Software faults are mostly caused by operators, and replicas cannot stop operator mistakes
Replication doubles the write load, and that extra load is itself what triggers the bug
The same systematic bug can affect every replica at the same time
Replicas lag behind the primary, so none of them can serve requests during a fault

questions.explanation: Hardware faults are usually random and independent, so a redundant copy is unlikely to fail at the same moment and can take over. A systematic software bug is different: the same code runs on every replica, so the same bad input or environmental event can crash them all simultaneously. These correlated faults cause many more system failures than uncorrelated hardware faults, and adding identical replicas does not help. Operator error is a separate class of fault, and replication lag does not stop failover in general.

questions.question: Which incident is an example of a systematic software fault, rather than a hardware fault or human error?

options.text: An operator's mistyped command that removed far more storage servers than intended
The June 2012 leap second, which hung many applications at once via a Linux kernel bug
A power failure in one datacenter rack that took its servers offline for several hours
A single disk dying in a 10,000-disk storage cluster, as expected about once a day

questions.explanation: A systematic fault is a bug present on many nodes that one shared event triggers everywhere at once. On June 30, 2012, a leap second activated a Linux kernel bug and caused many applications to hang simultaneously. A single disk dying or a rack losing power is a hardware fault that affects only the failed component or its rack. A mistyped operator command is human error, even if the software made it easy to do damage.

questions.question: Why do systematic software bugs 'lie dormant for a long time' before firing?

options.text: They wait for unusual circumstances that violate an assumption about their environment
They are introduced only during upgrades, so they fire on the next deployment after that
Compilers optimize them away entirely until the load rises above some threshold
They only trigger once the disk has filled up and writes have begun to fail

questions.explanation: A systematic bug may remain invisible while its hidden assumptions continue to hold. An unusual event—such as a leap second, resource exhaustion, or an unexpected dependency response—can violate one of those assumptions and activate the same defect on many nodes.

questions.question: One way to reduce human error is to design abstractions, APIs, and admin interfaces that make the right thing easy and the wrong thing hard. Which caveat applies?

options.text: That designing such interfaces costs far more than training people properly
That it works only for internal tools, never for customer-facing interfaces
That over-restrictive interfaces get worked around, negating the benefit
That it must always be paired with a formal certification programme

questions.explanation: Well-designed abstractions, APIs, and admin interfaces make it easy to do the right thing and discourage the wrong thing. But if the interfaces are too restrictive, people will work around them, which undoes the benefit. The designer has to balance guidance against flexibility. The caveat is about people bypassing controls, not about cost compared with training or about internal versus customer-facing tools.

questions.question: To keep the places where people make mistakes separate from the places where mistakes cause failures, teams provide non-production sandbox environments that do not affect real users. Which two properties should such a sandbox have? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Fully featured, so it exercises the real code paths
Using real data, so the behaviour observed is representative
Isolated on a separate physical network segment
Reset to a clean state automatically after every use

questions.explanation: The sandbox should be fully featured and use real data, while not affecting real users. Fully featured means experiments exercise the same code paths and mechanisms as production; real data means the behaviour observed is representative. Together they let people explore and experiment safely, so mistakes made while learning cause no failures for users.

optionExplanations.a: A fully featured sandbox runs the real code paths and operational mechanisms, so lessons transfer to production. A simplified toy can give false confidence because it omits exactly the behaviors that make changes risky.
optionExplanations.b: Representative real data exposes realistic distributions, edge cases, and interactions that synthetic examples may miss. It must still be protected and isolated so experimentation cannot affect real users.
optionExplanations.c: Isolation from real users is necessary, but it need not take the form of a separate physical network segment; logical access controls and environment boundaries can provide it. The properties that make the sandbox useful are realistic features and data.
optionExplanations.d: Automatic reset can be useful operationally, but resetting after every use is neither required nor sufficient for safe, representative experimentation. It could also erase state needed to investigate a multi-step scenario.

questions.question: Which levels of testing are needed, and what is automated testing especially valuable for?

options.text: Unit tests at the module level; valuable mainly as protection against regressions
Integration and load tests; valuable chiefly for catching performance regressions
Chaos tests in production; valuable mainly for validating that fault-tolerance machinery works
Unit through whole-system integration and manual tests; valuable for rare corner cases

questions.explanation: Testing should range from focused unit tests through whole-system integration tests, with manual tests where human judgment is useful. Automation is especially valuable for repeatedly exercising rare corner cases that normal operation may not reveal.

questions.question: Which three recovery mechanisms limit the impact of human error? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Fast rollback of configuration changes
Gradual rollout of new code, so bugs reach only a subset of users
Tools to recompute data, in case the old computation was incorrect
Mandatory review by a second engineer before any change ships

questions.explanation: Quick recovery limits the impact of a human error that has already happened. Fast configuration rollback undoes a bad config, gradual rollout limits how many users a bad code change reaches, and recomputation tools repair derived data produced by an incorrect computation. Each gives a different kind of reversibility: config, code, and derived data. Peer review is a preventive step taken before a change ships, not a way to recover afterwards.

optionExplanations.a: Fast configuration rollback shortens the duration of a harmful change by restoring a known-good state quickly. This limits impact after an error rather than trying to prove mistakes can never occur.
optionExplanations.b: A gradual rollout exposes only a small subset of users or machines before wider deployment. Monitoring can detect an unexpected bug while its blast radius is still limited.
optionExplanations.c: Recomputation repairs derived data when an earlier algorithm or input was wrong. Rollback alone cannot correct results already materialized, so rebuilding them provides a separate form of reversibility.
optionExplanations.d: Peer review may prevent some mistakes, but it is not a recovery mechanism that reverses a bad configuration, code rollout, or derived dataset. Reviews also cannot guarantee that every subtle failure is found before release.

questions.question: What do other engineering disciplines call monitoring, and what analogy fits?

options.text: Instrumentation, by analogy with the dashboard of a car
Telemetry, by analogy with a rocket that has left the ground
Auditing, by analogy with double-entry financial accounting
Observability, by analogy with a medical diagnostic scan

questions.explanation: In other engineering disciplines, detailed monitoring such as performance metrics and error rates is called telemetry. Once a rocket has left the ground, telemetry is essential for tracking what is happening and for understanding failures, since you cannot inspect it directly. Monitoring does the same for software: it gives early warning signals, shows whether assumptions or constraints are being violated, and helps diagnose a problem once it occurs.

questions.question: Which human-error mitigation depends primarily on organizational practice rather than data-system design?

options.text: Detailed and clear monitoring
Good management practices and training
Sandbox environments
Quick and easy recovery

questions.explanation: Good management and training shape how people make decisions, learn procedures, and respond under pressure. System design can still reduce mistakes through clear monitoring, safe sandboxes, and fast recovery, but it cannot replace those organizational practices.

questions.question: Under what circumstances may a team deliberately sacrifice reliability, and on what condition?

options.text: Never; even a prototype must meet the reliability bar of the production system
Only where a signed SLA explicitly permits a lower level of service to customers
To cut development or operating cost, as long as it is a conscious choice
Whenever the service's users are not paying for it, as no contract applies

questions.explanation: Reliability can be sacrificed to reduce development cost, for example when building a prototype for an unproven market, or operational cost, for example for a service with a very narrow profit margin. The condition is that the team is very conscious of when it is cutting corners. Even noncritical applications carry responsibility to users, so 'never' is too strong, while tying the decision only to SLAs or internal tools misses the cost trade-off.

questions.question: How is scalability defined, and why are both 'X is scalable' and 'Y doesn't scale' meaningless?

options.text: Coping with increased load; the useful question is how to cope with a given growth
Maximum sustainable throughput; the phrases fail because throughput is mismeasured
The ability to add machines; the phrases fail because any system can add machines
Capacity rising linearly with cost; the phrases fail because cost is never linear

questions.explanation: Scalability is a system's ability to cope with increased load. It is not a one-dimensional label, so calling a system scalable or not scalable says nothing. The useful questions are: if the system grows in a particular way, what are our options for coping with the growth, and how can we add computing resources to handle the additional load? Defining it as raw throughput, adding machines, or linear cost picks one mechanism and loses the 'which growth, which response' framing.

questions.question: Why must the current load on a system be described before its growth can be discussed?

options.text: Because current load is far easier to measure than any future growth
Because 'what if load doubles?' needs load parameters to answer
Because the growth rate tells you how many machines to buy up front
Because the load figure dictates which database you ought to choose

questions.explanation: Growth questions such as 'what happens if our load doubles?' only make sense relative to a description of today's load. That description is a few numbers called load parameters, for example requests per second or the ratio of reads to writes. Without them there is nothing to double. Ease of measurement, machine purchasing, and database choice are secondary to having a baseline.

questions.question: When describing the load on a system, what determines the best choice of load parameters?

options.text: Published industry benchmarks for your class of application
Requests per second, which is the right parameter for every kind of system
The guidance issued by your database vendor for that workload
Your system's architecture; sometimes a few extreme cases dominate

questions.explanation: The best load parameters depend on the system's architecture. They might be requests per second to a web server, the ratio of reads to writes in a database, the number of simultaneously active users in a chat room, or the hit rate on a cache. Sometimes the average case matters most; sometimes the bottleneck is dominated by a small number of extreme cases. No single parameter or outside benchmark fits every system.

questions.question: Using Twitter's published November 2012 numbers, what were the request rates for posting tweets and for reading home timelines, and what made scaling hard?

options.text: Post tweet 300k/sec, home timeline 4.6k/sec; the difficulty is write volume
Post tweet 4.6k/sec (12k peak), home timeline 300k/sec; the difficulty is fan-out
Post tweet 12k/sec, home timeline 45k/sec; the difficulty is storage volume
Post tweet 4.6k/sec, home timeline 30M/sec; the difficulty is network bandwidth

questions.explanation: Posting averaged 4.6k requests per second (over 12k at peak) while home-timeline reads ran at about 300k per second. Handling 12,000 writes per second would be fairly easy on its own. The challenge was fan-out: each user follows many people and is followed by many people, so a single tweet must reach many timelines and a single timeline read must gather tweets from many accounts.

questions.question: Where is the term 'fan-out' borrowed from, and what does it mean in transaction processing systems?

options.text: Fluid dynamics; the way load spreads out across partitions
Electronic engineering; requests to other services per incoming request
Broadcast radio; the number of receivers tuned to one transmitter at once
Graph theory; the length of the longest path leaving a vertex

questions.explanation: The term comes from electronic engineering, where fan-out counts how many gate inputs are driven by one output. In transaction systems it similarly measures how many downstream requests or writes one incoming operation creates; Twitter's follower distribution makes that multiplier highly uneven.

questions.question: In Twitter's fan-out-on-write timeline design, which metaphor best describes each user's precomputed home timeline?

options.text: A ledger of tweets, appended once per post and replayed in full on every read
A firehose of tweets, sampled per user when a timeline is requested
A mailbox of tweets, one per recipient user, filled at write time
A ring buffer of tweets, overwritten as newer posts arrive

questions.explanation: Fan-out on write treats each home timeline like a mailbox: when a tweet is posted, it is copied into the cached timelines of its followers. The alternative stores the tweet once and performs joins at read time, trading cheap writes for more expensive timeline reads.

questions.question: Why did Twitter move from assembling timelines at read time to precomputing most timelines at write time?

options.text: Home-timeline reads were far more frequent than new-tweet writes
Timeline reads were cheaper than writes, so work belonged on the read path
Storage costs had fallen enough to make all duplication insignificant
Relational databases could not index tweets by their author

questions.explanation: At roughly 4.6k new tweets versus 300k home-timeline reads per second, reads occurred about 65 times as often. Precomputing timelines moves work from the much hotter read path to the less frequent write path, although celebrity accounts require a hybrid exception.

questions.question: At roughly 4,600 tweets per second and 75 followers per tweet, what average write rate does fan-out on write create, and what celebrity-scale worst case must it handle?

options.text: About 345k writes/sec; over 30M writes for one tweet, within five seconds
About 345k writes/sec; worst case about one million writes, within one minute
About 4.6k writes/sec; worst case 30M writes, within five minutes
About 12k writes/sec; worst case 300k writes, within one second

questions.explanation: The average is 4,600 × 75 ≈ 345,000 timeline-cache writes per second. The average hides the tail: an account with more than 30 million followers can trigger over 30 million writes for one tweet, with a target of delivering them within about five seconds.

questions.question: When discussing the scalability of Twitter's home timelines, what is the key load parameter?

options.text: Tweets published per second, averaged across the whole day and every account
The distribution of followers per user, possibly weighted by tweet frequency
The total number of accounts that have ever been registered on the service
The ratio of home-timeline reads to tweet writes across the whole system

questions.explanation: The distribution of followers per user determines the fan-out load: how many timeline writes each tweet causes. The average hides the important part, because some accounts have over 30 million followers. Weighting by how often each user tweets makes the parameter reflect actual write load. The read-to-write ratio explains why work was moved to write time, but it does not reveal the skew that makes celebrity tweets expensive.

questions.question: After first assembling timelines at read time and then fanning tweets out at write time, Twitter moved to a hybrid. Which describes it?

options.text: All timelines computed at read time, backed by an aggressive cache
Fan-out at write time for celebrities, and read-time joins for everyone else
Timelines sharded by follower count, so large accounts get dedicated machines
Fan-out at write time, except celebrities, whose tweets are merged on read

questions.explanation: Most users' tweets are still fanned out to followers' home timelines when they are posted. A small number of users with very large follower counts (celebrities) are excepted: their tweets are fetched separately and merged into a follower's timeline when it is read. Reversing that assignment would put the most expensive fan-outs back on the write path. The hybrid keeps reads cheap for the common case while avoiding millions of writes per celebrity tweet.

questions.question: Once load is described by load parameters, increased load can be investigated in two ways. Which? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Increase a load parameter with resources unchanged, and ask how performance suffers
Ask how much you must add to resources to hold performance unchanged
Reduce the load parameter to zero and measure the system's idle cost
Compare your figures against a competitor's published benchmark

questions.explanation: The first experiment holds resources fixed and observes how performance degrades as load rises. The second adds resources until the original performance is restored. Both therefore require explicit performance measures such as throughput and response time.

optionExplanations.a: Holding CPU, memory, disk, and network resources fixed reveals how throughput or response time deteriorates as a named load parameter rises. It directly measures the system's current headroom and bottlenecks.
optionExplanations.b: Adding resources until performance returns to its prior level measures the scaling cost of growth. It answers whether capacity can be expanded reasonably rather than merely observing degradation.
optionExplanations.c: Measuring idle cost may help capacity accounting, but it says nothing about how the system responds when load increases. Scalability analysis requires varying a meaningful load parameter.
optionExplanations.d: A competitor's benchmark may use different workloads, data, and service objectives, so it does not characterize this system's response to growth. The required experiments relate its own load, resources, and performance.

questions.question: Which metric matters in a batch processing system such as Hadoop, and which in an online system?

options.text: Throughput for batch; response time for online
Response time for batch; throughput for online
Throughput for both, since each counts requests completed per second
Availability for batch; latency for online

questions.explanation: A batch system such as Hadoop is judged by throughput: the number of records processed per second, or the total time to run a job on a dataset of a given size. An online system is judged mainly by response time: the time between a client sending a request and receiving a response, because a user is waiting. Throughput matters for online systems too, but it does not tell you how long individual users wait.

questions.question: Distinguish latency from response time. Which one does the client see?

options.text: They are synonyms, and both describe what the client observes
Response time is what the client sees; latency is time spent awaiting service
Latency is what the client sees; response time is measured only server-side
Response time is the median; latency is the 99th percentile of the same data

questions.explanation: Response time is the end-to-end delay observed by the client, including service time, queueing, and network delays. Latency is the time a request spends waiting to be handled. Keeping the terms distinct prevents an end-to-end user metric from being confused with one component of it.

questions.question: Which causes make response times vary, even for identical repeated requests? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A context switch to a background process
Loss of a network packet and TCP retransmission, or a garbage collection pause
A page fault forcing a read from disk, or mechanical vibrations in the server rack
Variation in the CPU's advertised clock speed rating

questions.explanation: Even identical requests encounter different scheduling, network, garbage-collection, caching, page-fault, and storage conditions. Response time is therefore a distribution, and tail percentiles reveal delays that an average would conceal.

optionExplanations.a: The operating system may deschedule a request to run background work, adding queueing time even when the request itself is unchanged. Scheduling makes repeated response times a distribution rather than a constant.
optionExplanations.b: Packet loss triggers retransmission and garbage collection pauses application work; both add intermittent delays unrelated to the logical request. These rare stalls are precisely why tail percentiles matter.
optionExplanations.c: A page fault replaces a memory access with slow disk I/O, and physical vibration can disturb mechanical disks. Either can create occasional long responses even for otherwise identical operations.
optionExplanations.d: An advertised clock-speed rating is a static hardware specification, not a request-by-request event that explains latency variation. Dynamic effects may exist, but the label printed for the CPU does not fluctuate between identical calls.

questions.question: What is the objection to reporting average response time?

options.text: Computing a true mean over a rolling window is too expensive to do online
It hides how many users actually experienced a given delay
It is distorted by clock skew between the client and the server
It cannot be meaningfully aggregated across several machines

questions.explanation: An arithmetic mean compresses the entire distribution into one number, so it does not reveal how many users saw a particular delay or how severe the slow tail was. Percentiles answer that user-experience question, although percentiles cannot be averaged meaningfully across machines.

questions.question: A user's page load makes four requests to a service. Assuming their response times are independent draws from the service's response-time distribution, what is the probability that at least one is slower than the median?
questions.explanation: For one request, the chance of being no slower than the median is 0.5. Under the stated independence assumption, all four are no slower with probability 0.5⁴ = 6.25%, so at least one is slower with probability 1 − 0.5⁴ = 93.75%. Correlated requests would require a different calculation.

questions.question: A service's 95th percentile response time is 1.5 seconds. What does that mean?

options.text: The arithmetic mean of all requests measured in the window is 1.5 seconds
About 95% finished within 1.5 seconds and about 5% took longer
Every user sees exactly 1.5 seconds on 95% of their own requests
The single slowest request in the measurement window took 1.5 seconds

questions.explanation: A percentile is a threshold in a distribution, not an average. A p95 of 1.5 seconds means roughly 95% of observations are at or below that value and the slowest 5% exceed it.

questions.question: Amazon specifies internal service response times at the 99.9th percentile, affecting only 1 in 1,000 requests. What is the reasoning?

options.text: It is the cheapest percentile to compute on a live dashboard
It is the percentile least distorted by garbage collection pauses
The slowest requests often come from the most valuable, data-rich customers
Financial regulators require e-commerce firms to report at that particular percentile

questions.explanation: Amazon's customers with the slowest requests are often those with the most data on their accounts, because they have made many purchases, so they are the most valuable customers. Keeping the site fast for them protects revenue, which justifies a target even though it affects only 1 in 1,000 requests. The choice is about who sits in the tail, not about computation cost, garbage collection, or regulation.

questions.question: Which statements about response time and business outcomes are supported by reported measurements? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Amazon observed that a 100 ms increase in response time reduces sales by 1%
Others reported that a 1-second slowdown reduces a customer satisfaction metric by 16%
Response-time changes below one second have no measurable effect on revenue
Only average response time, not tail latency, correlates with customer satisfaction

questions.explanation: Reported measurements link small delays to business outcomes: Amazon observed that 100 ms of extra response time reduces sales by 1%, and others report that a 1-second slowdown reduces a customer satisfaction metric by 16%. These figures are why response time, including the tail, is treated as a business metric. Claims that sub-second changes do not matter, or that only the average matters, contradict them.

optionExplanations.a: Amazon observed that an extra 100 milliseconds of response time reduced sales by about 1%. It shows that even delays users barely notice consciously can have a measurable business cost.
optionExplanations.b: A reported result found that a one-second slowdown reduced a customer satisfaction metric by 16%. User-visible delay affects how customers judge a service, not just technical throughput.
optionExplanations.c: An extra 100 milliseconds was observed to cut sales by about 1%, so changes well below one second clearly can affect revenue. Assuming sub-second latency is irrelevant ignores that evidence.
optionExplanations.d: The slowest requests often belong to the customers with the most data and purchases, which is why Amazon sets targets at the 99.9th percentile. An average hides those users, so tail latency matters at least as much as the mean.

questions.question: Amazon optimizes p999 but deemed p9999 not worth it. For which two reasons? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Those response times are easily affected by random events outside your control
The benefits of further reduction are diminishing
Histogram approximation algorithms cannot estimate it accurately
Customers do not notice delays that far out in the tail

questions.explanation: At extremely high percentiles, measurements are dominated by rare events outside the service's control, while further improvement becomes disproportionately expensive and benefits fewer requests. Amazon therefore considered p99.9 worth optimizing but not p99.99.

optionExplanations.a: At p99.99, a tiny number of observations can be dominated by network hiccups or other rare events outside the service's control. Engineering the service cannot reliably remove all of those external causes.
optionExplanations.b: Each additional nine targets fewer requests while often requiring disproportionate cost and complexity. The marginal user benefit therefore shrinks, creating a rational stopping point for tail optimization.
optionExplanations.c: Approximate histograms can estimate very high percentiles when configured with enough range and precision. Measurement difficulty is real, but it is not why Amazon stopped at p99.9.
optionExplanations.d: Users experiencing extreme delays do notice them; tail latency can be especially painful because one slow dependency can delay a whole page. The decision reflects cost and controllability, not an assumption that those users are unaware.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes an SLO from an SLA?

options.text: An SLO is a target; an SLA is a customer agreement that may attach consequences
An SLO is a customer contract with financial penalties; an SLA is just an internal target
SLOs cover availability, while SLAs cover response time
They are interchangeable names for the same metric

questions.explanation: A service-level objective is a target such as median latency below 200 ms, p99 below one second, or 99.9% availability. A service-level agreement is a customer-facing agreement that can incorporate objectives and consequences. An SLO is not inherently restricted to internal use.

questions.question: An SLA promises the service is up at least 99.9% of the time. How much downtime does that permit in a 30-day month?

options.text: 4.3 minutes
43.2 minutes
7.2 hours
8.6 minutes

questions.explanation: A 30-day month has 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. An uptime of 99.9% allows 0.1% downtime, and 0.1% of 43,200 minutes is 43.2 minutes. Each additional nine cuts the allowance tenfold: 99.99% permits about 4.3 minutes per month.

questions.question: Why do queueing delays dominate high percentiles, and what practical consequence follows?

options.text: Slow requests hold up those queued behind them, so measure client-side
The network dominates the delay, so measure on the server side to exclude it
Collection pauses are periodic, so average over a much longer window
Disk seeks dominate, so the fix is to put a caching layer in front of storage

questions.explanation: A server can process only a small number of requests in parallel, limited for example by its CPU cores. A few slow requests can therefore hold up the requests queued behind them, an effect called head-of-line blocking. Those later requests may be fast to process, but the client still sees a slow response because of the wait. The server-side processing time misses that queueing time, so response times should be measured on the client side.

questions.question: When artificially generating load to test scalability, what must the client-side load generator do?

options.text: Throttle itself as responses slow, to avoid overloading the system under test
Keep sending independently of response time, or queues stay artificially short
Send from a single thread, so that the test is exactly reproducible
Reproduce the production read-to-write ratio as closely as possible

questions.explanation: A generator that waits for the previous response before sending the next one keeps the queues shorter in the test than in reality, which skews the measurements — hiding exactly the queueing effect you are trying to measure.

questions.question: You want percentiles on a monitoring dashboard. Which aggregation is wrong, and what is right?

options.text: Averaging percentiles is meaningless; add the histograms instead
Summing percentiles is wrong; average them across machines instead
Rolling windows distort percentiles; use fixed, non-overlapping windows instead
p999 is too noisy to display; report only p99 on dashboards instead

questions.explanation: Percentiles cannot be averaged across machines or time windows because each percentile has already discarded the underlying distribution. Aggregate the histograms or sketches first and calculate the percentile from the combined distribution; tools such as t-digest or HdrHistogram make this practical.

questions.question: How often must a fast-growing service revisit its architecture?

options.text: At least once a year, as part of capacity planning, whatever the growth rate
On every order of magnitude of load increase, or perhaps more often
Only once an SLA has actually been breached in production
Once, at the move from a single machine to a distributed system

questions.explanation: An architecture that is appropriate for one level of load is unlikely to cope with 10 times that load. A fast-growing service should therefore expect to rethink its architecture on every order-of-magnitude increase in load, or perhaps more often. Scalability is a moving target, not a property designed in once, and waiting for an SLA breach means rethinking only after users are hurt.

questions.question: What are scaling up and scaling out, and how do good architectures usually treat the choice between them?

options.text: Up adds machines, out adds CPUs to a machine; prefer scaling out
Up suits stateless services, out suits stateful ones; keep the two strictly separate
Up is a more powerful machine, out is many smaller ones; mix both in practice
Up is elastic, out is manual; prefer the elastic option where possible

questions.explanation: Scaling up is vertical scaling; scaling out is horizontal scaling, also called a shared-nothing architecture. Good architectures usually involve a pragmatic mixture of both: a few fairly powerful machines can be simpler and cheaper than a large number of small virtual machines.

questions.question: When is an elastic system useful, and what is the argument for manual scaling?

options.text: Elastic suits unpredictable load; manual is simpler with fewer surprises
Elastic is always preferable; manual scaling is a legacy practice
Elastic suits predictable load; manual scaling suits spiky load
Elastic is cheaper to run; manual scaling is the more reliable option

questions.explanation: Elastic systems automatically add resources when load rises, which is useful when demand is unpredictable. Manual scaling can be operationally simpler and more predictable because people control when disruptive actions such as repartitioning occur.

questions.question: Why is distributing a stateless service easy while distributing a stateful data system is not, and what 'common wisdom' followed?

options.text: Stateless services need consensus, so the wisdom was to shard databases early
Distributing state adds much complexity, so keep the database on one node
Stateful systems cannot be replicated, so the wisdom was to avoid databases
Stateless services are slower, so the wisdom was to cache aggressively

questions.explanation: Stateless instances can often be added or replaced independently because durable state lives elsewhere. Distributing a database also requires coordinating ownership, replication, consistency, and recovery, so a common strategy is to keep it on one node until scale or availability requirements justify that complexity.

questions.question: What is 'magic scaling sauce', and does it exist?

options.text: A generic, one-size-fits-all scalable architecture; it does not exist
Twitter's proprietary technique for handling celebrity fan-out in home timelines
A caching layer that makes any read-heavy system scale linearly
The standard combination of sharding plus asynchronous replication, which fits any load

questions.explanation: No such generic, one-size-fits-all scalable architecture exists. The architecture of systems that operate at large scale is usually highly specific to the application. The problem may be the volume of reads, of writes, of data to store, the complexity of the data, the response time requirements, the access patterns, or some mixture.

questions.question: Compare a system designed for 100,000 requests/sec of 1 kB each with one for 3 requests/min of 2 GB each. What follows?

options.text: The first has 100x the throughput, so it needs roughly 100x the machines
The second is the easier system, because it handles far fewer requests
Both move about 100 MB/s, yet the two systems look nothing alike
Throughput is the only load parameter that matters for either system

questions.explanation: 100,000 x 1 kB/s is 100 MB/s; 3 x 2 GB/min is 6 GB/min, also 100 MB/s. Identical on that metric, utterly different in design — so throughput alone does not determine architecture.

questions.question: A scalable architecture assumes which operations are common and which are rare. What should an early-stage product do about that?

options.text: Design for a thousand times the expected load from the first release, to avoid rewrites
Wrong assumptions waste the effort, so iterate on product features first
Pick a NoSQL database early, to keep the scaling options open
Hire a dedicated scalability team before the product launches

questions.explanation: If those assumptions are wrong the scaling effort is at best wasted and at worst counterproductive; iterating on features beats scaling to some hypothetical future load. Even so, scalable architectures are built from general-purpose building blocks arranged in familiar patterns.

questions.question: Where does the cost of software actually live?

options.text: Most cost is initial development, so ship fast and rewrite later
Most cost is infrastructure and hosting, which outweigh engineers' salaries
Most cost is testing, which is why it is the first thing teams cut
Most cost is ongoing maintenance, not the initial development

questions.explanation: Maintenance includes fixing bugs, investigating failures, adapting to new platforms and use cases, repaying technical debt, and adding features. Because this work continues for most of a system's life, maintainability usually dominates its total cost rather than the initial implementation.

questions.question: Why is it hard to give general recommendations for dealing with legacy systems?

options.text: Every legacy system is unpleasant differently, so aim not to create one
Legacy systems are typically undocumented, so advice has nothing to build on
A full rewrite is the standard answer, so there is little else to recommend
Legacy maintenance is a management problem, not an engineering one

questions.explanation: Legacy systems accumulate different combinations of constraints, dependencies, and historical decisions, so a universal repair recipe is unlikely to fit. A more general defense is to design new systems for operability, simplicity, and evolvability, reducing future maintenance pain.

questions.question: Simplicity as an engineering goal means 'make it easy for new engineers to understand the system, by removing as much complexity as possible'. Which clarification belongs with that definition?

options.text: That it is not the same as user-interface simplicity
That simplicity requires reducing functionality
That simplicity must be traded off against reliability
That simplicity only applies to code, not to data models

questions.explanation: This is internal simplicity: engineers should be able to understand the system's state, behavior, and interactions without carrying unnecessary complexity in their heads. It is independent of whether the product's user interface looks simple.

questions.question: A well-known claim says that good operations can often work around the limitations of bad or incomplete software, but good software cannot run reliably with bad operations. What does this imply about operations and automation?

options.text: Operations should be fully automated so that software, not people, keeps it running
Operations is vital; humans must still set up and check the automation
Bad software cannot be rescued by any amount of operational skill
Good automation makes a dedicated operations team unnecessary for most systems

questions.explanation: Operations teams are vital to keeping a system running smoothly. Some aspects of operations can and should be automated, but it is still up to humans to set up that automation in the first place and to make sure it is working correctly. Automation does not remove the need for operations people; it changes what they spend their time on.

questions.question: Which responsibility of a good operations team is about the organization rather than the machines?

options.text: Monitoring the health of the system and quickly restoring service
Preserving the organization's knowledge as individual people come and go
Keeping software and platforms up to date, including security patches
Establishing good practices for deployment and configuration management

questions.explanation: Preserving organizational knowledge means documenting systems, decisions, and operational practices so service reliability does not depend on particular individuals remaining on the team. It is an organizational continuity responsibility rather than a machine-maintenance task.

questions.question: Which ways can data systems make routine operational tasks easy? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Providing visibility into runtime behaviour and internals, with good monitoring
Avoiding dependency on individual machines, so machines can be taken down
Behaving predictably, with good defaults that administrators can still override
Hiding all configuration knobs, so operators cannot set anything incorrectly

questions.explanation: Data systems make routine operations easy by providing visibility through good monitoring, supporting automation, avoiding dependency on individual machines so they can be taken down for maintenance, providing good documentation, behaving predictably, and offering good defaults that administrators can override. Self-healing is useful where appropriate, but administrators should still have manual control over system state. Hiding every knob removes exactly that control.

optionExplanations.a: Monitoring and visibility let operators understand internal state, diagnose failures, and verify recovery instead of guessing. Observability turns routine maintenance into an informed, repeatable process.
optionExplanations.b: When service health does not depend on one named machine, operators can replace or maintain machines without a special outage. Redundancy and automated failover make hardware lifecycle tasks routine.
optionExplanations.c: Predictable behavior and safe defaults reduce surprises, while override controls let experts handle unusual situations. Operability requires both automation for the common case and agency for exceptions.
optionExplanations.d: Removing every configuration control prevents operators from responding when automation chooses badly or a novel failure occurs. Good defaults are valuable, but they are paired with manual control rather than enforced helplessness.

questions.question: A software project mired in complexity is sometimes called a 'big ball of mud'. Which of these are symptoms of such complexity? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Explosion of the state space, and tight coupling of modules
Tangled dependencies, and inconsistent naming and terminology
Hacks aimed at performance, and special-casing to work around issues
Slow build times and unusually large deployment artifacts

questions.explanation: A big ball of mud is a system whose structure has become obscured by tangled dependencies, tight coupling, inconsistent concepts, performance hacks, and special cases. Those forms of complexity enlarge the state space developers must reason about; slow builds alone do not define the condition.

optionExplanations.a: A huge state space and tightly coupled modules multiply the interactions developers must reason about. A local change can affect distant behavior, which is a defining form of accidental complexity.
optionExplanations.b: Tangled dependencies and inconsistent terminology obscure the system's conceptual structure. Engineers cannot reliably predict behavior when the same idea has several names or modules depend on one another unpredictably.
optionExplanations.c: Performance hacks and issue-specific branches accumulate exceptions to the normal design. Each special case weakens general rules and makes future changes harder to understand and test.
optionExplanations.d: Slow builds and large artifacts can be painful, but they are not signs of conceptual complexity in themselves. They may come from project size or tooling even when the architecture stays clear and easy to reason about.

questions.question: Why does complexity increase the risk of bugs, not merely slow people down?

options.text: Hidden assumptions and unexpected interactions get overlooked more easily
More lines of code mean proportionally more defects per release
Complex systems resist automated testing, so bugs escape to production
Complex systems tend to attract less experienced engineers

questions.explanation: When a system is harder for developers to understand and reason about, hidden assumptions, unintended consequences, and unexpected interactions are more easily overlooked when making a change. The risk comes from what people cannot see, not from a fixed defect rate per line of code. Reducing complexity therefore improves maintainability and makes changes safer.

questions.question: Simplifying a system does not necessarily mean reducing its functionality. How do Moseley and Marks define the accidental complexity that simplification removes?

options.text: Complexity introduced by a bug that nobody has yet found and fixed
Complexity that arises only from the implementation, not from the users' problem
Complexity that arrives with third-party dependencies, which you cannot simplify yourself
Complexity that only becomes visible once the system is under load

questions.explanation: Complexity is accidental if it is not inherent in the problem the software solves, as seen by the users, but arises only from the implementation. Because users never asked for it, removing accidental complexity costs no features. The other options describe bugs, dependencies, or load-dependent behaviour, which can contribute to complexity but are not the definition.

questions.question: Why is abstraction the best tool for removing accidental complexity, and what is the second-order benefit?

options.text: It reduces the number of lines of code, cutting bugs proportionally
It removes layers of indirection between components, so the system runs faster
It hides detail behind a clean facade, and reuse spreads fixes to every user
It lets a smaller team maintain the same amount of functionality

questions.explanation: A good abstraction hides a great deal of implementation detail behind a clean, simple-to-understand facade. It can also be reused across many applications, which is more efficient than reimplementing the same thing, and quality improvements in the abstracted component benefit every application that uses it. Abstraction is about hiding detail, not removing indirection or merely cutting lines of code.

questions.question: What does SQL abstract?

options.text: Machine code, CPU registers and operating system calls
Storage structures, concurrent requests, and inconsistencies after crashes
Network protocols, serialization formats and wire compatibility between versions
Schema evolution, data migrations and rolling upgrades

questions.explanation: SQL hides the complex on-disk and in-memory data structures that store the data, the concurrent requests arriving from other clients, and the inconsistencies a crash could otherwise leave behind. Users state the result they want rather than coordinating those mechanisms themselves. Machine code, CPU registers and system calls are what a high-level programming language hides, and wire formats and schema migrations are separate concerns that SQL does not take off your hands.

questions.question: Abstraction is not a solved technique. What is the honest state of the art, specifically for distributed systems?

options.text: Good abstractions are hard to find, especially for distributed systems
Distributed systems need only good algorithms, not new ways of packaging them
Every abstraction leaks under heavy load, so they are best avoided entirely
SQL already provides the right abstraction for distributed systems

questions.explanation: Finding good abstractions is very hard. In distributed systems there are many good algorithms, but it is much less clear how to package them into abstractions that keep the complexity of the whole system manageable. So the gap is in packaging, not in a lack of algorithms, and abstractions remain worth seeking rather than avoiding.

questions.question: Agile already offers TDD and refactoring. Why is 'evolvability' needed as a separate word?

options.text: Agile methods do not apply to data systems in any form
Refactoring addresses only code style, never system structure
Evolvability is nonfunctional, whereas agility is a functional requirement
Those techniques work at a small local scale; a larger system needs its own word

questions.explanation: TDD and refactoring help code change locally; evolvability names the same ability at system scale, where several services, schemas, dataflows, and teams must change without excessive risk. The separate term keeps system-level changeability visible as a design goal.

questions.question: Requirements split into functional and nonfunctional ones. Which of the following count as nonfunctional? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Security and reliability
Compliance and scalability
Compatibility and maintainability
Storing, retrieving, searching and processing data

questions.explanation: Functional requirements describe what the application does, such as storing, retrieving, searching, and processing data. Security, reliability, compliance, scalability, compatibility, and maintainability instead constrain how well or under what conditions it performs those functions.

optionExplanations.a: Security and reliability constrain how safely and dependably the application performs its functions. They describe qualities of operation rather than a user-visible data operation such as storing or searching.
optionExplanations.b: Compliance constrains permitted behavior and scalability constrains how the system handles growth. Both are cross-cutting qualities, not individual functions the application exposes.
optionExplanations.c: Compatibility governs interaction across versions, while maintainability governs how productively people can operate and change the system. These are properties of the implementation over time.
optionExplanations.d: These are things the application must do for its users, which is what a functional requirement describes. Nonfunctional requirements describe qualities such as security or scalability that apply across those functions.

questions.question: How are faults commonly classified by their source, and how does scalability relate to reliability?

options.text: Hardware, software and human faults; scalable systems add capacity to stay reliable
Transient, permanent and Byzantine faults; reliability is a prerequisite for scale
Network, disk and CPU faults; scalability and reliability are independent concerns
Detected and undetected faults; high load always reduces reliability

questions.explanation: Faults are classed as hardware faults (typically random and uncorrelated), software faults (bugs that are typically systematic and hard to deal with), and human errors. Scalability links back to reliability because in a scalable system you can add processing capacity in order to remain reliable under high load. The other options use fault taxonomies from other contexts or treat the two concerns as unrelated.
